To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. Synaptic organization in the visual (but not olfactory) input region of the ant's mushroom bodies changes in a way that is associated with behavioral transition and light‐exposure, 2. This change in synaptic organization is driven by visual experience and not by an internal program, and 3. This structural plasticity may be related to the behavioral transition from brood care to outdoor foraging.

(i) The volume of the MB calyces in foragers increases by 50% compared to interior workers, (ii) the number of MGs per calyx decreases by 50% in foragers compared to interior workers and (iii) this decrease is due to presynaptic pruning in projection neurons and to postsynaptic dendritic growth of Kenyon cells.
1) The number of microglomeruli (MG), synaptic complexes in the mushroom body calyx, decrease during the behavioral transition from interior worker to forager.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how synaptic plasticity in sensory centers of the ant's brain contributes to the behavioral transition associated with the division of labor.
the question of how the brain of the desert ant, Cataglyphis, is able to adapt to the transition of the worker ants from a life as interior worker to a life as forager.
the structural synaptic plasticity of the mushroom bodies of desert ants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MBs of the desert ant C. fortis are plastic in their synaptic organization.

synaptic plasticity in MB calyces of desert ants is driven primarily by visual experience rather then by an internal program and that it may be an important mechanism related to behavioral transitions associated with division-of-labor.
the visual experience of the ant has a strong influence on the structural synaptic organization of the MB calyces and that this plasticity is age‐related.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mushroom bodies (a sensory integration center supposed to be involved with learning and memory) of the desert ant undergoes synaptic plasticity in response to changes in visual input.
the mushroom body of the desert ant is a very plastic brain region, and that it is not just a matter of learning, it is also a matter of experience.
we show that the mushroom bodies of desert ants are highly plastic and that visual experience is a key factor for this plasticity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
visual experience affects synaptic organization in the visual input region of the mushroom bodies (a learning and memory center) of the desert ant, Cataglyphis.
the brain of the desert ant, Cataglyphis, is able to adapt its synaptic structure to changes in the environment.

synaptic plasticity in visual regions of the mushroom bodies (the brain center for sensory integration and learning and memory) is driven by visual experience and age rather than by an intrinsic program.
